Explain the concept of economic growth and economic development. How do indicators like national income and per capita income measure a country's progress? Highlight their limitations in reflecting holistic development. (800 words) Ans. Economic activity is essentially an attempt to strike-out a balance between unlimited wants and scarce resources. A nation consists of many economic ecosystems which impact the lives of its citizens. So, to calculate the change in economic activity and its impacts over a specific period of time, economists came up with concepts of economic growth and development. Both are similar concepts but differ largely in their perspective, scope, measurement and implications for a nation. Economic growth is the change in the total value of goods and services produced in a period of time compared to a base year. It is a quantitative parameter to gauge a country's improvement. Some of the methods used to measure economic growth are Gross Domestic Product, Gross National Product etc. Economic Growth basically measures the scale of economic activity going on in a country. It constitutes factors like infrastructural development, jobs created, exports etc. While economic development is more of a qualitative parameter to measure a country's journey for its betterment. It focuses on evaluating the overall well-being of individuals. Economic growth is mere a subset of economic development. It measures the improvement in factors like education, healthcare, access to resources etc and checks if issues like illiteracy, high mortality rate are waning over a period of time. Economic development focuses on human factor more than money factor. Some tools to measure it are Human Development Index, Gross Happiness Index etc. National Income and per capita income are important indicators of economic growth. National Income is the total value of products and services generated in a country over a period of time. Higher national income means an increased production and economic strength. It also tells the size of economy and production capacity of a nation. Per capita Income is national income divided by the total population. It shows the living standard of inhabitants of a country. It determines the average income for each individual. In most scenarios, more per capita income means better access and availability of resources. Although there are some anomalies when it comes to relying on indicators like national income and per capita income. For example, if there was an earthquake in a country and considerable work went into repairing roads, and buildings, and restoring the damage caused. In this case, national income could falsely appear to have increased while it is a setback not progress. Indicators like National income and per capita income do not bother about lives lost or injuries. Some of the limitations of national income and per capita income are: a. Hiding inequality—These indicators do not account for the distribution of income in an economy. World Inequality Labs reported that the top 1% rich in India have 22% income while the bottom 50% have only 15% income. Even if a country's per capita income is high, it does not ensure everyone's access to resources.

Poverty is a complex phenomenon with multiple dimensions extending beyond economic hardship. Discuss the concept of poverty, its various types, and how these dimensions influence human capital, societal well-being, economic capabilities of individuals in India. (600 words) Ans. Poverty is a state in which an individual is deprived of basic needs like nutrition, income, education, and health. Though often poverty is interchanged with the people's income unavailability, it is a multifaceted concept that looks after an individual's basic needs, including education, health, living standards, and the income they generate. Adding to this, World Bank, highlighted that $2.15 per day is the extreme poverty line. Though, all other aspects are also calculated using Multidimensional Poverty Index in India. The types of poverty that prevail are 1. Absolute Poverty- It is the threshold of the country that the individuals earning below the specified poverty line are called poor. It generally looks for income earned by them and calorie consumption. For Example, In India Rs. 1059 per month and Rs 1286 per month is the poverty line in Rural and Urban areas respectively. 2. Relative Poverty- Poverty where an individual is compared to the other section of society in terms of income and living standards. For Example- People living in slum areas are considered poor as compared to the ones living in the main cities. 3. Generational Poverty- The poverty that is transferred from one generation to the other. Exemplifying- People in slum areas transfer poverty to their young ones, which can not be avoided. They lack education facilities, improper health facilities, etc. 4. Situational Poverty- When because of certain situations people become poor is the certain poverty. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many people lost their jobs, and because of this, they became poor. Providing certain assistance can help them come out of such type of poverty. 5. Multidimensional Poverty- When any individual lacks in three areas, which are Education, Health, and Living Standard, is said to be known as multidimensional poor. Though, Multidimensional Poverty focuses not only on the monetary indicators but also on the education, health, and living standards. It stated a person living in a rural area if earns less than Rs 27 per day and one living in an urban area earns less than Rs 33 per day, then is said to be known as Poor. This was the poverty line given by him. But is this seriously a poverty line or a destitution line? The answer to this question lies in the flaws it had. 1. Focus on Income factors- Tendulkar Committee focused primarily on the income generated by the individuals. It neglected factors like sanitation, quality education, better health facilities, etc.

The National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) 2024 by NITI Aayog highlights "24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty in the last nine years" between 2013-14 to 2022-23. Critically analyze the factors driving this reduction, the shortcomings of MPI, and suggest a way forward for accurate poverty measurement and alleviation. (800 words) Ans. The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) is a measure of poverty that takes into consideration the parameters of health, education and living standards to give us a comprehensive idea about the progress our economy has made in terms of poverty mitigation. Globally, it was developed by Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative along with UN Development Programme. In India, it is released by the NITI Aayog. As per the recent estimates, poverty has reduced by 18% between 2013-14 and 2022-23. The reduction in poverty rate to 11.28% can be attributed to several factors, they are: a) Economic growth - After the reforms in liberalization, privatization and globalization India has performed satisfactory in achieving an adequate average economic growth of 7% in the following years. This growth has helped in job creation in formal sectors and providing good wages to the employees. This has brought improvement in the living standards of people. b) Education - The education system in India has improved in comparison to early years. The gross enrolment ration has increased in primary education and efforts are being made to raise it in higher education also. Improvement in infrastructure has also encouraged students to attend school. Literacy will make people more aware about benefits they can avail themselves from various domains and can also understand law in a better to fight against injustice. c) Better health services - The set up of primary health centres and community health centres in rural areas has made health services accessible to people in the rural areas. This has provided primary health check-up for people, which has also promoted better human capital in the economy. d) Nutrition - The Government has started giving food items at a lower price rate to the targetted beneficiaries in India through the Public Distribution System. The PM-POSHAN scheme also provides meal to the school going children. These initiatives help to provide adequate nutrition to the children and will make their immunity strong which will help them to fight against any diseases. The better upbringing of the children will also produce efficient human capital in the economy. e) Equality - Gender inequality has made the lives of the women miserable as they fail to get access to the basic need of life. Setting policies for empowering women and increasing female literacy rates have helped many women to work on their own and become independent. This has also made them to fight against poverty. f) Tax reforms - The government has introduced Goods, Services and Tax in 2017. This has brought huge reforms in the tax sector. The tax rate calculation and collection have become transparent, which has reduced tax evasion. Better revenue collection by the government has promoted developmental activities in the economy, which will contribute to improve the lives of the people. The shortcomings of MPI are:

Unemployment is defined as a situation where a person is capable of working but is unable to get a job. In India, involuntary unemployment is a major issue. As per the PLFS report (July 2023 - June 2024), the unemployment rate in India for both male and females aged 15 years and above was 3.2%. As a subcontinent home to 1.45 billion people, this percentage depicts crores of people outside the workforce and their potential being untapped. Unemployment exists in India in several forms, such as: 1. Disguised Unemployment: Often evident in the agricultural or unorganized sector, this type of unemployment occurs where more people are employed than actually required. 2. Seasonal Unemployment: Arise when people become jobless as need for labor decreases. For instance, resort employees are laid off in off season or agricultural laborers turn jobless when it's not the growing season. 3. Structural Unemployment: It occurs due to structural changes in the economy, such as change in technology (from labour intensive to capital intensive) or due to change in pattern of demand. Here, a person fails to grasp the opportunity due to mismatch in his skills and qualifications and the availability of jobs in the market. 4. Frictional Unemployment: When people switch jobs or search for a new one, the brief period of unemployment that arises is referred to as frictional unemployment.
